newsitem.title: USA: Dollar eases on rising Japan trade surplus, U.S. stock slide.
newsitem.headline: Dollar eases on rising Japan trade surplus, U.S. stock slide.

text.p: The dollar eased against the yen on Wednesday after Japan said its trade surplus more than doubled in May, heightening concern about rising exports to the United States.
The dollar also retreated against the mark -- after extending its recent rally to a new 3-1/2-year high -- with a selloff on Wall Street eroding support late in the day.
Japan reported that its May current account surplus, the broadest measure of trade and often a source of friction with the United States, jumped 155 percent to 907 billion yen.

The surplus, although near market expectations, eventually weighed on the dollar as speculators bet that the Japanese and U.S. governments might resort to pushing up the value of the yen to make Japanese goods more expensive in the United States.
"It backed off on the realisation that it is still a widening trade surplus," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange trading manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

Japanese economists and Finance Ministry officials have expressed the view that the surging surplus was due to a hefty increase in exports, which rose 20 percent in May, powered especially by car shipments to the United States.
U.S. manufacturers continue to complain that their competitive edge has been eroded by a strong dollar this year.

Remarks at a San Francisco meeting of the Japan-U.S. Business Council on Tuesday from Ford Motor Co. Vice Chairman Wayne Booker also pressured the U.S. currency. Booker called for a weaker dollar exchange rate against the yen.

But the dollar's decline was surprisingly subdued and Japanese officials were quick to say the flood of exports would be soon counterbalanced by a pickup in imports after the effects of a recent consumer tax hike wears off.

"With the actual number coming in pretty much with people's expectations, plus the comments from Ministry of Finance officials indicating it was just a temporary fluctuation ... it really did temper concern that you could get a reignition of the trade war," said Anne Pankowski, a vice president at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
The Dow Jones industrial average was down almost 170 points during the afternoon, which often prompts investors to lighten their dollar holdings.
The dollar ended at 112.75 yen, down from 112.85 at Tuesday's close and at 1.7605 marks, off from 1.7612.

In early New York trade, the dollar rose to 1.7650 marks, its highest since February 1994, mostly as a result of continued mark selling by investors concerned that Europe will replace the German currency with a broad-based, but weak single currency as planned in 1999.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4580 Swiss francs from 1.4645 on Tuesday. It eased to Canadian $1.3737 from C$1.3745.
